tagline: A rainbow-coloured boxer with a spring-loaded punch
summary: This vividly coloured reef crustacean smashes snails and crabs with club-like forelimbs that strike faster than almost any other animal movement. Its eyes are among the most complex known — though, contrary to popular belief, that doesn't mean it sees colours better than we do.

stats.range: Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to the Mariana Islands
stats.diet: Snails, crabs and other crustaceans, clams

facts.title: A punch with a spring
facts.text: A saddle-shaped spring in each striking limb stores energy, then releases it in a blow reaching 14–23 m/s with accelerations of 6,300–8,000 times gravity — one of the fastest feeding strikes known.

facts.title: Every strike hits twice
facts.text: The club moves so fast that it creates cavitation bubbles — pockets of vapour that collapse violently. Force sensors recorded a second peak from the collapsing bubbles a fraction of a millisecond after the impact itself.

facts.title: Up to 16 kinds of light sensors
facts.text: Mantis shrimp eyes contain between 12 and 16 types of photoreceptor (light-sensing cells), with about 12 devoted to colour, spanning ultraviolet to far red. Humans have four types.

facts.title: Myth: they see more colours
facts.text: Despite all those receptors, colour tests found mantis shrimps are surprisingly poor at telling similar colours apart — worse than humans. More receptors does not mean a richer palette.

facts.title: Colour by scanning?
facts.text: Researchers proposed that mantis shrimps recognise colours quickly by sweeping their eyes across a scene, rather than finely comparing them as we do. This idea is still being tested and debated.
